introduction-why-regex-isnt-enough.core: Regex sees text, so it can't tell code from comments or strings, or know what a name refers to. Linters that parse code into a syntax tree understand structure and give precise, reliable rules.

first_principles.problem: A regex for `eval(` flags comments and strings and misses `e = eval; e(x)`, with false positives and negatives everywhere.
truths: Parsers already exist for every language.

analogy.title: Auditing logs for a word vs. understanding events
analogy.story: Searching for 'unauthorized' finds comments and jokes; parsing access events finds the actual violations.
analogy.breaks: An AST shows syntax, not runtime behaviour. Dynamic tricks can still evade it.

check.q: Why does regex produce false positives for code rules?
check.a: It matches text inside comments and strings, without understanding code structure.

the-abstract-syntax-tree-ast.core: Parsing turns source text into a tree of typed nodes (Module → FunctionDef → Call → Name). Python's `ast` module exposes it, and a NodeVisitor walks it to find patterns.

first_principles.problem: To analyse code reliably you need its structure, not its characters.
truths: Each construct has a node type with fields.
derivation: Subclass **ast.NodeVisitor** and define visit_Call and friends.

analogy.title: Sentence diagramming
analogy.story: Breaking a sentence into subject, verb and object shows its structure, whatever the punctuation.
analogy.breaks: The AST drops comments and formatting. For those you need a CST (libcst).

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only real eval calls are reported, with line numbers.

check.q: What Python class helps you walk an AST with per-node-type methods?

writing-a-pylint-plugin.core: Packaging an AST rule as a Pylint checker plugin gives you standard message IDs, consistent output, disable comments and editor integration, instead of a one-off script.

first_principles.problem: Standalone scripts have custom output, no suppression mechanism and no IDE integration.
truths: Suppression is needed for justified exceptions.
derivation: Declare **msgs** with an ID and symbol (W9001, no-eval).

analogy.title: Adding a new inspection to an existing checklist
analogy.story: Instead of a separate clipboard, the new check joins the inspector's standard form.
analogy.breaks: Pylint uses astroid (an enriched AST), so APIs differ slightly from the stdlib ast.

example.title: A no-requests-without-timeout rule
example.outcome: custom rules feel like built-in ones.

check.q: Why write a Pylint plugin instead of a standalone script?
check.a: It gives standard output, suppression comments, configuration and IDE/CI integration for free.

integrating-custom-linters-into-cicd.core: A rule that isn't enforced is only a suggestion. Run custom linters in pre-commit for fast feedback and as a required CI check, and roll them out with baselines so existing violations don't block everyone.

first_principles.problem: A new rule would fail 300 existing files on day one, so the team disables it.
truths: Fast local feedback reduces CI failures.
Legacy code needs a migration path.
derivation: Add a **CI job** as a required status check.
Use a **baseline or diff-only** mode for legacy code.
Track **violations over time** down to zero.

analogy.title: New building codes
analogy.story: New construction must comply immediately, while existing buildings get a phased deadline.
analogy.breaks: Too many blocking rules frustrate developers, so keep the rules high-value.

example.title: A GitHub Actions lint job

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: New violations are blocked while legacy ones are fixed gradually.

code.text:
- name: Custom lint
  run: |
    git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- '*.py' \
      | xargs -r pylint --load-plugins=lint.timeout --disable=all --enable=requests-no-timeout

example.outcome: rules are enforced without a revolt.

check.q: How do you introduce a strict rule into a large legacy codebase?
check.a: Enforce it only on changed code or against a baseline, then burn down existing violations over time.

advanced-patterns-detecting-attribute-ca.core: Real rules have to match attribute calls (`os.system`), aliased imports (`import subprocess as sp`, `from os import system`) and keyword arguments. Track imports to resolve names before matching calls.

first_principles.problem: A rule that only catches `os.system(...)` misses `from os import system as run; run(cmd)`.
truths: Code reaches the same function through many names.
Calls have positional and keyword arguments.
derivation: **visit_Import / visit_ImportFrom** to build an alias map.
**visit_Call**: resolve **Attribute** chains or **Name** through the alias map.
Resolve to a **qualified name** before matching.

analogy.title: Tracking nicknames
analogy.story: To know 'Bobby' is Robert, you need the introductions (imports) before the conversation (calls).
analogy.breaks: Fully dynamic access (getattr, importlib) still evades static analysis.

example.title: Detecting subprocess with shell=True

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: It catches `sp.run(cmd, shell=True)` even with an alias.

example.outcome: rules robust to how code is written.

check.q: Why track imports in a custom linter?
check.a: To resolve aliases so the rule recognises the same function under different names.
